mygit: Go CLI plan & architecture

What to build to turn the my-git Claude plugin into a standalone Go CLI: features, architecture, config files, git/gh/agent integration and day-to-day usage.

  • Updated2026-11-14
  • Scopeagentic-workflows · develop/feat/my-git @ 2a3b817
  • StatusProposal, not built yet

The plan in one screen

Recommendation

Build mygit as one Go binary in plugins/my-git/cli. Move all rule logic into it, and turn everything else into thin callers of the binary: Claude Code hooks, Codex and Antigravity adapters, git hooks and skills. Today the rules live in the Python gitguard package, and a second copy is hard-coded into the git-hook shell templates. S1S2

  1. One engine, many entry points. The same Go rule engine (rule ids ID*, CM*, BR*, GH* kept as they are) answers the agent hooks, git hooks, mygit lint and mygit commit / pr. S3
  2. Named profiles instead of one flat profile. A global config holds several profiles, such as personal and work. Each project picks one, either explicitly or through match rules. mygit profile use writes the matching git config and switches the gh account. INFERRED design proposal: today's profile is a single set of variables. S4
  3. Four JSON layers, later wins: built-in defaults → global ~/.config/mygit/config.json → project .mygit.json (committed) → project-local .mygit.local.json (git-ignored). Environment variables and flags sit on top.
  4. git and gh are called as subprocesses. mygit adds no git library and no GitHub API client, so your existing credentials, SSH config and gh auth keep working unchanged.
  5. Agents talk to mygit through a small adapter protocol: mygit guard --agent claude|codex|agy|json. Claude Code's format is known from the current hook. S5 The Codex and Antigravity hook formats still need checking. OPEN
  6. Plan first, always. Every command that changes something does a dry run by default: it prints a numbered plan, the exact commands and the rule checks, and changes nothing. In auto mode (the default) mygit runs the plan once it's approved, either by you or by the agent after showing it to you. In manual mode it prints the commands for your shell, and you run them yourself.
  7. Windows shells are first-class. Manual-mode output is rendered separately for PowerShell (the default on Windows), cmd and Git Bash. The Windows code is written in the implementation phases, but there is no Windows test setup yet. OPEN
  8. Signed commits by profile. Each profile chooses ssh, gpg, x509 or none. mygit sign sets the key up, uploads it to GitHub through gh and verifies signatures. A new rule, ID006, blocks unsigned commits when the profile asks for signing.
  9. See the repo. mygit graph draws the commit graph with origin/* branches, ahead/behind counts, signatures and PRs. mygit flow draws the branching workflow (work branches → develop/base → main) with live state.
  10. Rules have scopes, like profiles. Named rule sets are defined globally or per project and selected the same way as profiles. Single-rule overrides apply at the global, project or local level on top of the chosen set.
  11. Git workflow templates. The branching model is a template: branches, naming, start points, which branch a PR may go into, merge style, protection and release steps. mygit ships one built-in default (today's main + develop/base model). You can add custom templates globally, per project or locally, and they are selected the same way as profiles and rule sets. The active template drives the BR rules, branch / pr commands, the GitHub ruleset and the flow view.
4 → 1rule copies today (Python engine, sh hooks, skills, PR template) → one Go engine
35existing rules carried over (ID 5 · CM 16 · GH 9 · BR 5)
7build phases, each shippable on its own

What exists today and what is missing

my-git already does most of the policy work, as a Claude Code plugin written in Python. S6 What it lacks is a standalone tool: named profiles, a real config hierarchy, and support for agents other than Claude, all of which your target list asks for. S7

Your goal features compared with the current plugin (branch develop/feat/my-git @ 2a3b817)

Multi-scope JSON config (global + per project)~ Profile has 2 scopes. Rules are customised by ejecting a whole contract file into .claude/git-guard/contracts/. S9One schema at every scope; deep-merge; override a single rule by id; mygit config show --origin

How the CLI is put together

Everything that decides anything lives in one binary. The outer layer only translates: it turns an agent's hook payload, a git hook's arguments, or your command line into a call to the core. The core turns that into git and gh subprocesses.

Go package layout

The core modules map one-to-one onto Go packages under cli/internal/. The shipped contracts are embedded in the binary with go:embed, so a fresh install works without any files on disk.

cli/
  go.mod                         module …/mygit   (Go 1.23+)
  cmd/mygit/main.go              wires cobra commands
  internal/
    cli/          one file per command group (profile, config, commit, pr, repo, hooks, agent, guard, lint, doctor)
    config/       schema, load layers, deep-merge, origin tracking, validate
    profile/      select (explicit → match rules → default), apply to git config / gh auth
    rules/        identity.go commitmsg.go branching.go ghpolicy.go   (ports of scripts/gitguard/*)
    engine/       Evaluate(cmd, dialect, cwd, cfg) → Verdict       (port of gitguard/engine.py)
    shell/        bash via mvdan.cc/sh/v3/syntax; PowerShell tokenizer ported from shellparse.py
    gitx/ ghx/    thin os/exec wrappers: Run, Query, JSON; dry-run + trace
    plan/         Plan{id, steps[read|write], checks}; build → show → apply; plan id = hash(argv + repo state)
    shellfmt/     render a plan for posix (bash/zsh), gitbash, powershell, cmd: quoting, env, paths, chaining
    sign/         ssh / openpgp / x509 setup, allowed_signers file, verify (%G?), key upload via gh
    graph/        lane layout of the commit DAG; terminal + SVG/HTML renderers; flow (workflow) view
    workflow/     template schema, built-in "default", extends/merge, select by scope, compile → BR rule params,
                  branch/PR routing, GitHub ruleset, flow layout, PR templates per transition
    tmpl/         text/template for commit msg, PR body, hook shims, agent files
    agent/        adapters: claude, codex, agy, json   (Decode stdin → Request, Encode Verdict → stdout/exit)
  defaults/       embedded: contracts/*.json, templates/*, schema.json
  testdata/       golden hook payloads + expected verdicts (ported from tests/*.py)

Mapping from the Python code to Go packages S1

Python todayGo packageNote
gitguard/engine.pyinternal/engineSame flow: pre-filter → parse → per-program checks → strictest severity wins
gitguard/shellparse.py, commands.pyinternal/shellBash: use a real parser (mvdan.cc/sh) INFERRED it covers what the 455-line hand parser does; check against the existing tests
identity.py, commit_message.py, branching.py, gh_policy.pyinternal/rulesKeep rule ids and params, so existing overrides still apply

How the config files work

Every scope uses the same JSON schema. mygit loads the layers in order and deep-merges them, and a later layer wins. Personal values (who you are) live only in the global file and the git-ignored local file. The committed project file holds only team conventions, so the repo never names a person. The current contracts follow the same principle. S13

Global config: your profiles

Path: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mygit/config.json, falling back to ~/.config/mygit/config.json on macOS and Linux and %APPDATA%\mygit\config.json on Windows. The profile fields are today's profile variables, grouped. S14

{
  "$schema": "https://…/mygit/schema/v1.json",   // also: mygit config schema > schema.json
  "version": 1,
  "defaultProfile": "personal",
  "profiles": {
    "personal": {
      "git":    { "name": "Octo Cat", "email": ["1234+octocat@users.noreply.github.com"],
                  "signing": { "format": "ssh", "key": "~/.ssh/id_sign.pub" } },
      "github": { "user": "octocat", "orgs": [], "transport": "gh" }
    },
    "work": {
      "git":    { "name": "Octo Cat", "email": ["octo@acme.example"], "signing": { "format": "default" } },
      "github": { "user": "octo-acme", "orgs": ["acme"], "transport": "ssh", "sshKey": "~/.ssh/id_acme" }
    }
  },
  "match": [                                        // first hit wins, before defaultProfile
    { "remoteOwner": "acme",     "profile": "work" },
    { "path": "~/work/**",       "profile": "work" }
  ],
  "execution": { "mode": "auto", "shell": "auto" },  // auto = powershell on Windows, $SHELL elsewhere
  "rules": { "CM009": "off" }                       // personal taste, every repo
}

Comments here are only for reading. The real file is plain JSON. Supporting JSONC comments is an open question.

Project config: team conventions

Path: <repo root>/.mygit.json, committed. It holds today's contract settings and rule overrides in one place, so you no longer need to eject a whole contract. S15S9

{
  "version": 1,
  "commit": {
    "convention": "conventional",
    "types":  ["feat","fix","docs","refactor","perf","test","build","ci","chore","revert"],
    "scopes": ["api","cli","ui"],                    // empty = any scope
    "headerMax": 72,
    "forbidAiAttribution": true,
    "template": ".mygit/commit.tmpl"                 // optional, else built-in
  },
  "workflow": "default",                           // or a custom template: see "Git workflow templates"
  "pr": {
    "base": "auto",                                // from the workflow's transitions
    "sections": ["Summary","Detailed changes","Explanation","Test results"],
    "template": ".github/pull_request_template.md",
    "checks": { "test": "go test ./...", "lint": "golangci-lint run" }
  },
  "github": { "owners": ["acme"], "ruleset": { "approvals": 1 } },
  "ruleset": "team",                               // a named rule set (see "Rules have scopes")
  "rules": {
    "CM007": { "params": { "max": 72 } },
    "GH006": "deny"
  },
  "agents": ["claude", "codex"],
  "execution": { "mode": "auto" }                  // a project may force "manual"
}

Project-local config and merge rules

<repo>/.mygit.local.json is git-ignored. mygit init adds it to .gitignore. It usually holds a single line, {"profile": "work"}, and can override anything else for you alone.

How a value is resolved

KindRuleExample
ScalarLast layer that sets it winscommit.headerMax: built-in 72 → project 100
ObjectDeep-merged key by keyProject branch.staging keeps global branch.remote
ArrayReplaced, not appendedProject commit.types is the full list
rulesPer rule id. A string is shorthand for severity, an object merges severity and params"CM009": "off"
profilesAllowed only in global and local layers. In .mygit.json they are a validation errorKeeps people out of committed files
rulesetsDefined in the global or project layer, and in local for personal ones. Selected like a profileSee the next section
workflowsCustom templates in the global, project or local layer, selected like a profileSee "Git workflow templates"
${var} in rule paramsResolved from the active profile, same semantics as today"expected_logins": ["${github.user}"] S16
Invalid configAs today, an invalid file must not silently turn the guard off. The agent adapter answers ask for every git or gh command until the file is fixed, and mygit doctor names the file, line and field. S5

Rules have scopes, like profiles

A rule set is a named bundle of rule severities and params, such as strict, team or solo. It is defined and selected the same way as a profile. On top of the selected set, each layer can still override single rules by id.

Which rule set is active?

First hit wins: --ruleset → MYGIT_RULESET → local "ruleset" → project "ruleset" → global match → global defaultRuleset → built-in default (today's contracts).

Then per-rule overrides

rules maps merge on top in layer order: global → project → local → env → --rule ID=severity. A set can extends another set.
// ~/.config/mygit/config.json  (personal rule sets)
"rulesets": {
  "solo":   { "extends": "default", "rules": { "BR005": "warn", "GH008": "ask" } },
  "strict": { "extends": "default", "rules": { "ID006": "deny", "CM009": "deny", "CM010": "deny" } }
},
"defaultRuleset": "solo",
"match": [ { "remoteOwner": "acme", "profile": "work", "ruleset": "strict" } ]

// .mygit.json  (team rule set, committed)
"rulesets": { "team": { "extends": "strict", "rules": { "CM007": { "params": { "max": 100 } } } } },
"ruleset": "team"
$ mygit rules show --origin CM007 ID006 CM009
CM007  deny  max=100   ruleset team (.mygit.json) ← extends strict ← default
ID006  deny            ruleset strict (~/.config/mygit/config.json)
CM009  off             override rules.CM009 (.mygit.local.json)
$ mygit rules set CM009 warn --local      # dry-run plan, then apply
$ mygit rules use strict --local          # just for me, in this repo
Guard railThe global file may hold "locked": ["CM016", "BR002", "ID006"]. A lower layer or a rule set may make a locked rule stricter but never weaker, so a cloned project can't silently switch off your own safety rules. OPEN whether this should be the default.

Plan first: dry-run, auto mode and manual mode

In shortEvery command that changes something first builds a plan and stops there. Auto (the default) means mygit runs the plan after approval: yours, or the agent's after it has shown the plan to you. Manual means mygit prints the plan as commands for your shell, and you run them.

What a plan looks like

$ mygit commit -a -t feat -s auth -m "add login endpoint"
plan 7f3a2c   dry-run · mode auto · profile work · ruleset team · shell powershell
  1  read   git status --porcelain=v2                     3 files changed
  2  write  git add -A
  3  write  git -c user.name="Octo Cat" -c user.email=octo@acme.example
                -c gpg.format=ssh -c user.signingkey=~/.ssh/id_sign.pub commit -S -F <msg>
  checks  ✓ CM003 ✓ CM007 ✓ ID001 ✓ ID002 ✓ ID006 signed ✓ BR001 on develop/feat/login
apply? [y/N]

How each caller gets from plan to result

CallerAuto modeManual mode
You in a terminalPlan, then apply? [y/N]. --yes skips the promptPlan + copy-paste script for your shell
AgentRuns mygit … --json → shows you the plan → runs mygit … --apply 7f3a2c. The guard turns --apply into ask unless execution.agentApply is "allow"The agent hands you the script and does not run it
git hookNever plans: hooks only check (mygit hook …)

The mode and shell are config like everything else (execution.mode, execution.shell), so they follow the scopes: global default auto, a project may force manual, and --mode/--shell apply to one run.

Manual mode on Windows: one plan, three shells

In auto mode the shell doesn't matter: Go's os/exec starts git.exe and gh.exe directly with an argument list. The shell matters only for the text manual mode prints. On Windows the default is PowerShell. The commit message always goes through a file (-F) that mygit writes during planning, so no shell has to quote a multi-line message.

PowerShell (default)

git -C 'C:\src\api' -c user.name='Octo Cat' commit -S -F "$env:TEMP\mygit-7f3a2c.msg"

cmd

git -C "C:\src\api" -c user.name="Octo Cat" commit -S -F "%TEMP%\mygit-7f3a2c.msg"

Git Bash

git -C '/c/src/api' -c user.name='Octo Cat' commit -S -F "$TEMP/mygit-7f3a2c.msg"

What internal/shellfmt changes per shell

ConcernPowerShellcmdGit Bash / bash / zsh
Literal string'…', quote doubled ''"…"; ^ escapes & | < > ^; % doubled in scripts'…', quote as '\''
Set env for a step$env:GIT_SSH_COMMAND='…'set "GIT_SSH_COMMAND=…"GIT_SSH_COMMAND='…' git …
Stop on first failureone step per line + if (-not $?) { exit 1 } (works on 5.1 and 7)|| exit /b 1set -e at the top
Line continuationbacktick `^\
PathsC:\…C:\…/c/… (Git Bash), native elsewhere
Save as script--out plan.ps1--out plan.cmd--out plan.sh
Windows statusThe Windows code is written during the implementation phases: %APPDATA% config path, .exe lookup, the three renderers, hook shims (Git for Windows runs hooks with its own sh, so the same shim works) and PowerShell parsing in the guard. The renderers are pure string functions, so their golden tests can run on macOS. Nothing has been run on a real Windows machine, and there is no Windows CI yet. OPEN INFERRED PowerShell 5.1 quoting of native arguments is the most likely source of bugs, which is why messages go through -F files.

How a profile turns into git and gh settings

A profile is a declaration. mygit profile use applies it, and every later check verifies it. Applying writes repo-local git config (never --global unless you pass --global) and switches the active gh account.

What each profile field does

Profile fieldApplied withChecked by
git.name, git.emailgit config user.name / user.emailID001, ID002 on every commit
git.signingcommit.gpgsign=true, gpg.format=ssh, user.signingkeymygit doctor
github.transport = ssh + sshKeycore.sshCommand="ssh -i KEY -o IdentitiesOnly=yes"ID003, ID004
github.transport = ghgh auth setup-git; remote rewritten to HTTPSID003 (credential helper), ID004
github.usergh auth switch --user USERID005 before every gh call
github.orgs-ID004, GH006 allowed owners

Which profile is active? It is the first match in this list: --profile flag → MYGIT_PROFILE → .mygit.local.json profile → global match rules (by origin owner, then by path glob) → defaultProfile. If nothing matches, the identity rules fall back to presence checks, as they do today. S17

$ mygit profile use work
plan 1c9e04  dry-run · 5 writes · apply? [y/N] y
✓ git config user.name       Octo Cat
✓ git config user.email      octo@acme.example
✓ git config core.sshCommand ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_acme -o IdentitiesOnly=yes
✓ gh auth switch --user octo-acme
✓ wrote .mygit.local.json    {"profile": "work"}
remote origin git@github.com:acme/api.git → owner acme ✓ allowed

Commit signing

Signing belongs to the profile, because the key belongs to the account. mygit pins the signing settings on each commit with -c flags, as the commit skill does today, so a different global git config can't leak in. S19

git.signing.format and what mygit sets up

Formatgit config pinned per commitUpload to GitHub (mygit sign setup --upload)Local verify needs
ssh (recommended)gpg.format=ssh, user.signingkey=<.pub>, commit -Sgh ssh-key add KEY.pub --type signing INFERRED needs gh scope admin:ssh_signing_keygpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile, which mygit writes to ~/.config/mygit/allowed_signers; git ≥ 2.34
openpgpgpg.format=openpgp, user.signingkey=<key id>gh gpg-key add pub.ascgpg on PATH (Windows: the one bundled with Git or Gpg4win)
x509gpg.format=x509, gpg.x509.program=…-That program
defaultLeave git's own signing config, add -S-Whatever git is set up with
noneUnsigned--
  • Rule ID006 (new, identity contract): if the active profile has a signing format other than none, a git commit without -S, or with --no-gpg-sign or -c commit.gpgsign=false, is denied. Default severity: deny in strict, warn in default.
  • mygit sign verify [range] reads git log --format=%H%x1f%G?%x1f%GS and lists unsigned or bad commits, for example before a PR. mygit pr create runs it on the PR range.
  • mygit repo protect --require-signed adds the required_signatures rule to the GitHub ruleset.
  • If signing fails (locked agent, wrong passphrase), mygit stops and shows the error. It never retries without -S, which matches today's skill. S19

Commit, branch and PR rules: one engine, three ways in

The same rule check runs whether you or an agent type git commit, whether git fires its commit-msg hook, or whether you run mygit commit. Only the entry point differs.

Before the command

mygit guard sees the command line an agent wants to run and checks every rule (identity, message, branch, gh) before anything happens.

Inside git

.githooks/commit-msg → mygit hook commit-msg "$1". Catches you too, in any terminal or IDE.

On GitHub

A ruleset applied by mygit repo protect: PR required, no force-push, no deletion. S12

Templates

Templates are Go text/template files. Built-in ones are embedded. A project can point commit.template or pr.template at its own file. mygit commit fills the template from flags or prompts, then validates the result with the same rules, so a template can never produce a message the rules reject.

# built-in commit template
{{.Type}}{{if .Scope}}({{.Scope}}){{end}}{{if .Breaking}}!{{end}}: {{.Subject}}
{{if .Body}}
{{.Body}}{{end}}
{{range .Trailers}}
{{.}}{{end}}

The PR body uses the section names from pr.sections. mygit pr create pre-fills Test results with the actual output of pr.checks.test and pr.checks.lint, which the /my-git:pr skill asks the agent to do by hand today. S11

Git hooks become shims

mygit hooks install sets core.hooksPath=.githooks and writes three files that only forward to the binary:

#!/bin/sh
# .githooks/commit-msg — generated by mygit; logic lives in `mygit hook`
exec mygit hook commit-msg "$@"
EffectChanging commit.headerMax in .mygit.json takes effect at once, both in the agent guard and in git's own hook. Nothing needs re-rendering. If mygit is not on PATH, the shim prints an install hint and exits 0, so a teammate without mygit is never locked out. OPEN Should it fail closed instead?

Git workflow templates

In shortA workflow template is one JSON document that describes the branching model. mygit ships one built-in template, default, which is today's model. Custom templates live at the same scopes as profiles and rule sets (global, project, local) and can extends another template. Exactly one template is active per repo, and everything branch-related is compiled from it.

The built-in default template

It encodes what contracts/branching.json and the /my-git:pr skill do today. S15S11

{
  "name": "default",
  "description": "main (production) + develop/base (staging); work branches develop/<type>/<name>",
  "remote": "origin",
  "branches": {
    "production": { "name": "main",         "protected": true },
    "staging":    { "name": "develop/base", "protected": true, "githubDefault": true }
  },
  "work": {
    "pattern": "develop/{type}/{name}",
    "types":   "{commit.types}",                 // reuse the commit types
    "from":    "staging"
  },
  "transitions": [
    { "id": "merge",   "from": "work",    "to": "staging",    "via": "pr", "mergeMethod": "squash",
      "prTemplate": "default", "deleteHead": true },
    { "id": "release", "from": "staging", "to": "production", "via": "pr", "mergeMethod": "merge",
      "prTemplate": "release", "tag": "v{version}" }
  ],
  "protection": { "requirePr": true, "approvals": 0, "forcePush": false, "deletion": false,
                  "requireSigned": false, "linearHistory": false },
  "prTemplates": {
    "default": { "sections": ["Summary","Detailed changes","Explanation","Test results"] },
    "release": { "sections": ["Summary","Included PRs","Test results"] }
  }
}

Custom templates and scope

Templates are defined and selected with the same rules as profiles and rule sets, so there is only one mental model to learn.

Where templates live and how one is chosen

ScopeWhereTypical use
built-inembedded defaultWorks with no config at all
global~/.config/mygit/config.json → "workflows": {…}, or files in ~/.config/mygit/workflows/*.jsonYour personal model for side projects
project.mygit.json → "workflows", or .mygit/workflows/*.json (committed)The team's model, shared through the repo
local.mygit.local.json → "workflow" / "workflows"Try a template on your machine first

Which template is active? First hit wins: --workflow → MYGIT_WORKFLOW → local "workflow" → project "workflow" → global match (by owner or path) → global defaultWorkflow → built-in default. When names clash, the more specific scope wins (local > project > global > built-in), and mygit workflow show --origin tells you which file it came from.

// .mygit/workflows/release-train.json  (project, committed): a custom template
{
  "name": "release-train",
  "extends": "default",                         // inherit everything, change what differs
  "branches": {
    "staging": { "name": "develop" },
    "release": { "name": "release/{version}", "protected": true, "pattern": true }
  },
  "work": { "pattern": "{type}/{ticket}-{name}" },
  "transitions": [
    { "id": "merge",   "from": "work",    "to": "staging",    "via": "pr", "mergeMethod": "squash" },
    { "id": "cut",     "from": "staging", "to": "release",    "via": "branch" },
    { "id": "release", "from": "release", "to": "production", "via": "pr", "mergeMethod": "merge", "tag": "v{version}" },
    { "id": "backport","from": "release", "to": "staging",    "via": "pr" },
    { "id": "hotfix",  "from": "production", "to": ["production","staging"], "via": "pr", "work": "hotfix/{name}" }
  ],
  "protection": { "approvals": 1, "requireSigned": true }
}

// .mygit.json
{ "workflow": "release-train" }

Merge rules for extends: objects deep-merge, and transitions merge by id (same id replaces, new id is added, "remove": true drops one).

What the active template drives

$ mygit workflow show
workflow release-train   (.mygit/workflows/release-train.json ← extends default)
  production  main                 protected
  staging     develop              protected · GitHub default
  release     release/{version}    protected
  work        {type}/{ticket}-{name}   from staging
  merge     work       → staging       PR · squash · delete head
  cut       staging    → release       branch
  release   release    → production    PR · merge · tag v{version}
  backport  release    → staging       PR
  hotfix    production → production, staging   PR · work hotfix/{name}
  protect   PR required · 1 approval · signed commits · no force-push · no deletion
$ mygit workflow use release-train --project     # plan: update .mygit.json, ruleset, default branch
Switching on a live repomygit workflow use is a plan like everything else. It lists the branches to create, the GitHub default branch to change, the ruleset to replace, and existing work branches that no longer match the new pattern. It never renames or deletes branches by itself. Those steps appear in the plan as suggested commands for you to approve or run.

Working with gh

mygit never calls the GitHub REST API directly. It shells out to gh, so login, tokens, enterprise hosts and proxies are all handled by gh. Before any gh call, the core checks that the active gh account is the profile's github.user (ID005). S1

mygit commands and the gh calls behind them

mygitgh underneathOrigin
mygit repo create acme/api --privategh repo create acme/api --private --source . --pushsetup_repo.py github --create S10
mygit repo protect [--approvals N]gh api repos/{r}/rulesets (POST, or PUT if it exists); default branch; delete merged branchessetup_repo.py github
mygit pr create [--draft]gh pr list --head … --json url → gh pr create --base … --body-file …/my-git:pr S11
mygit pr releaseSame, head develop/base → base main/my-git:pr --release
mygit pr check <num>gh pr view N --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName → GH005/GH008/GH009/BR005check_pr.py
mygit profile usegh auth switch --user …, gh auth setup-gitnew

Seeing the repo: graph and workflow views

There are two read-only views built from the same data. mygit graph answers "what is where": commits, local and origin branches, and what is signed. mygit flow answers "where is each piece of work in the branching model, and what is the next step". Both print to the terminal, and with --html they write an offline page.

mygit graph

$ mygit graph --limit 10
* a1f9c02 (HEAD → develop/feat/login)         feat(auth): add login endpoint   ✔ ssh   ↑2 not on origin
* 77be310                                       feat(auth): add session store    ✔ ssh
│ * 5c0d1e9 (origin/develop/fix/timeout)        fix(api): raise client timeout   ✔ ssh   PR #18 open · checks ✓
├─╯
* 3e21aa0 (develop/base, origin/develop/base) ⛨  Merge pull request #16           ✔ github
│ * 9d4410b (main, origin/main) ⛨               Merge pull request #15 release   ✔ github
├─╯
* 0b7c1d4                                       chore: bootstrap repository      ✗ unsigned
legend  ⛨ protected (BR001/BR002) · ↑ ahead / ↓ behind origin · ✔ signature ok · ✗ unsigned/bad

Where each piece of the graph comes from

ShownSource command
Commits, parents, refs, signature statusgit log --all --topo-order --format=%H%x1f%P%x1f%D%x1f%G?%x1f%s, laid out into lanes by internal/graph (no --graph text parsing)
origin/* branchesIncluded via --all. --fetch first runs git fetch --prune origin, which is a write to refs and so goes through the plan/mode flow
Ahead / behindgit for-each-ref --format=%(refname:short)%x1f%(upstream:track)
Protected markerProtected branches from the active workflow template
PR number and checksgh pr list --state open --json number,headRefName,baseRefName,isDraft,statusCheckRollup (skipped offline)

mygit flow

Plugging into AI agents

Each agent gets three things. A pre-command hook calls mygit guard. Skills now just say "run mygit commit" instead of re-describing the rules. The git hooks act as the backstop. mygit agent install <agent> writes all three.

What mygit agent install writes per agent

AgentPre-command hookSkills / instructionsStatus
Claude CodePlugin hooks.json: PreToolUse Bash|PowerShell → mygit guard --agent claude; SessionStart → mygit guard --agent claude --session-start S18Existing commit, push, pr, git-guard skills, slimmed down to call mygitVERIFIED format in use today
Codex CLICodex hook config, if your Codex version offers a pre-exec hook; else noneSkill folder + an AGENTS.md block: "use mygit commit / mygit pr create"OPEN confirm Codex's hook event and payload
Antigravity CLISame approach, if agy exposes a pre-command hookagy skill/rules file pointing at mygitOPEN confirm agy's extension points
Any other toolmygit guard --agent json: JSON in, JSON out, exit code 0 allow · 1 ask · 2 deny-Generic fallback
Why git hooks matter hereWhen an agent has no pre-command hook, git's commit-msg and pre-push still run mygit hook. The agent sees the rejection in the command's stderr and fixes the message. You lose the identity and gh checks before the command runs, but commit and branch rules still hold.

Using the CLI

Commands are grouped by noun. Every command that changes something does a dry run by default and needs approval or --apply <plan-id> to run. Every command accepts --json, so agents can parse the output.

mygit   global flags: --workflow NAME  --mode auto|manual  --shell powershell|cmd|gitbash|bash|zsh  --apply [id]  --yes
                      --json  --profile NAME  --ruleset NAME  --rule ID=severity
├── init      [--workflow NAME]  create .mygit.json (+ .gitignore entry), suggest a profile, rule set and workflow
├── doctor                       git/gh versions, config validity, identity, signing, hooks, agent installs, shell
├── profile   list | show [name] | add <name> [--from-current] | edit <name> | rm <name>
│             use <name> [--global] | current | import   (from the git-guard profile files)
├── sign      setup [--format ssh|openpgp|x509|default|none] [--key PATH] [--upload] | status | verify [range]
├── rules     list | explain <ID> | show [--origin] [IDs…] | sets | use <set> [--project|--local]
│             set <ID> <severity> [--global|--project|--local] | view
├── workflow  list | show [name] [--origin] | use <name> [--global|--project|--local]
│             new <name> [--from default] [--global|--project] | validate [file] | diagram [--html out.html]
├── config    get <key> | set <key> <value> [--global|--project|--local] | show [--origin] | schema | validate
├── commit    [-t type] [-s scope] [-m subject] [--body …] [--breaking] [-a]          (signed per profile)
├── branch    new <type> <name> | cut <transition> [version] | prune       (patterns from the workflow)
├── push      [--upstream]        (never --force)
├── pr        create [--draft] [--to BRANCH] | release | run <transition> | check [num] | template
├── repo      create <owner/name> --private|--public | protect [--approvals N] [--require-signed] | bootstrap
├── graph     [--remote origin] [--limit N] [--fetch] [--html out.html]
├── flow      [--fetch] [--html out.html]
├── plan      show <id> | verify <id> [--out plan.ps1|.cmd|.sh]
├── lint      msg <text|-f file> | pr --title … --body-file … | cmd "<shell command>"
├── hooks     install | uninstall | status
├── hook      commit-msg|pre-commit|pre-push …         (called by git, not by you)
├── agent     install|uninstall <claude|codex|agy> [--scope project|user] | status
└── guard     --agent <claude|codex|agy|json>          (called by agents; reads stdin)

First-time setup on a machine

$ brew install mygit                      # or: go install …/mygit/cmd/mygit@latest
$ mygit profile add personal --from-current
  captured git user.name/email, gh login octocat, transport gh, signing: default
$ mygit profile add work --github-user octo-acme --ssh-key ~/.ssh/id_acme --org acme
$ mygit config set match '[{"remoteOwner":"acme","profile":"work"}]' --global
$ mygit sign setup --format ssh --key ~/.ssh/id_sign --upload
$ mygit agent install claude --scope user
$ mygit doctor
✓ git 2.47  ✓ gh 2.63  ✓ config valid (2 files)  ✓ signing ssh  ✓ shell powershell  ✓ claude hooks installed

New project

$ mkdir api && cd api && git init
$ mygit init --workflow default          # or a custom one: --workflow release-train
$ mygit repo bootstrap                    # first commit on main, create develop/base
$ mygit repo create acme/api --private    # profile "work" picked by owner match
$ mygit repo protect --approvals 1        # ruleset: PR-only main + develop/base
$ mygit hooks install                     # core.hooksPath=.githooks, 3 shims

A normal change

$ mygit branch new feat login --yes
✓ develop/feat/login (from develop/base)
$ mygit commit -a -t feat -s auth -m "add login endpoint"
plan 7f3a2c  …3 steps, all checks ✓…  apply? [y/N] y
✓ a1f9c02 feat(auth): add login endpoint   signed ssh (Good)
$ mygit pr create
plan 2b81de  dry-run · mode auto
  1 read   go test ./...                 → 42 passed
  2 read   golangci-lint run             → clean
  3 read   mygit sign verify develop/base..HEAD → 2/2 signed
  4 write  git push -u origin develop/feat/login
  5 write  gh pr create --base develop/base --head develop/feat/login --title … --body-file …
apply? [y/N] y
✓ https://github.com/acme/api/pull/17   develop/feat/login → develop/base

The same change in manual mode (Windows)

PS C:\src\api> mygit commit -a -t feat -s auth -m "add login endpoint" --mode manual
# plan 7f3a2c · manual · shell powershell · run these, then: mygit plan verify 7f3a2c
git -C 'C:\src\api' add -A
if (-not $?) { exit 1 }
git -C 'C:\src\api' -c user.name='Octo Cat' -c user.email='octo@acme.example' `
    -c gpg.format=ssh -c user.signingkey='C:\Users\octo\.ssh\id_sign.pub' `
    commit -S -F "$env:TEMP\mygit-7f3a2c.msg"
if (-not $?) { exit 1 }

Add --shell cmd or --shell gitbash for the other two shells, or --out plan.ps1 to save the script.

What a block looks like

$ mygit lint cmd 'git commit -m "Added stuff."'
✗ deny  CM003  header must be '<type>(<scope>)!: <subject>'
  try:  git commit -m "feat: add stuff"
$ echo $?
2

An agent sees exactly the same findings in its hook response, worded as an instruction it can act on. mygit rules explain CM003 prints the rule's description and its good and bad examples, taken from the contract. S15

Build order

Each phase ships something usable, and the Python plugin keeps working until phase 4 replaces its hook command.

  1. Skeleton, config, plan coreweek 1

    go mod init, cobra, internal/config (4 layers, schema, config get/set/show --origin). internal/plan with dry-run as the default, --apply, plan ids, and auto/manual mode. internal/shellfmt for posix, Git Bash, PowerShell and cmd, with golden tests that run on macOS. Windows paths and .exe lookup are written now. Embed today's contracts/*.json.

  2. Profiles + signingweek 1–2

    profile add/list/show/use/import, match rules, applying profiles to git config and gh. sign setup/status/verify for ssh, openpgp and x509, the allowed-signers file, and key upload through gh.

  3. Rules engine, rule scopes, lintweek 2–3

    Port the four rule groups and the shell parser, and add ID006. Rule sets with extends, locked, and rules use/set/show --origin. internal/workflow: template schema, built-in default, scoped selection, extends, validation, and compiling to BR params. Exit criterion: the default template gives the same BR verdicts as branching.json today. Port tests/*.py to Go table tests. Exit criterion: every Python test case gives the same verdict.

  4. Hooks: git + Claudeweek 3

    hook, hooks install (shims), guard --agent claude including the --apply → ask policy. Switch hooks/hooks.json to mygit, then delete the duplicate regexes in the templates.

  5. Workflow commands + ghweek 4

    commit, branch new/prune, push, pr create/release/check, repo create/protect/bootstrap, all built as plans and routed by the workflow template. workflow list/show/use/new/validate, transition commands (branch cut, pr run), and a ruleset per template. Slim the skills so they show the plan and then --apply.

  6. Graph + flow viewsweek 5

    internal/graph lane layout, terminal renderer (Unicode, plus an ASCII fallback for old Windows consoles), --html renderer, and flow laid out from the active workflow template plus gh pr list.

  7. More agents + releaseweek 6

    agent install codex|agy once their hook formats are confirmed, and guard --agent json. goreleaser builds for darwin, linux and windows (amd64/arm64). The Windows binaries are built but not tested. Homebrew tap. Retire scripts/.

Riskiest portThe shell parser: 455 lines handling bash -c, chains, quoting and PowerShell. mvdan.cc/sh covers bash. PowerShell has no Go parser, so its tokenizer must be ported by hand and tested against the existing test_shellparse.py cases.

Open questions

  • OPEN Ship more built-in templates? The current plan ships only default. GitHub flow, gitflow and trunk-based could ship as example custom templates (mygit workflow new --from-example gitflow) rather than built-ins.
  • OPEN Merge method enforcement. Should mergeMethod per transition also restrict the allowed merge methods in the GitHub ruleset? Rulesets set this per branch, not per source branch.
  • OPEN Windows test setup. When to add a windows-latest CI runner, and which PowerShell is the baseline: 5.1 (built in) or 7.
  • OPEN Agents and --apply. Proposed default: the guard asks you before an agent applies a plan. Set execution.agentApply: "allow" to let the agent apply after it has shown you the plan.
  • OPEN Plan expiry. Should a plan id also expire after some time, on top of the repo-state hash?
  • OPEN Codex and Antigravity hooks. Do the versions you run offer a pre-command hook, and what payload and response do they expect? This decides between a full guard and git-hook-only for those agents.
  • OPEN May a project loosen a rule? For example, can .mygit.json set CM016 to off? One option is a global "locked": ["CM016","BR002"] list that lower layers cannot weaken.
  • OPEN JSON or JSONC. Plain JSON is strict and fits the goal. JSONC allows the comments shown in the examples above.
  • OPEN Git-hook shim without mygit installed: fail open (current proposal) or fail closed?
  • OPEN Keep the Python plugin as a fallback after phase 6, or remove scripts/ completely?
  • OPEN Distribution: Homebrew tap only, or also go install and a plugin-bundled binary that Claude's hook can find through ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin?
